newsitem.title: UK: LME copper, zinc pare losses, others little change.
newsitem.headline: LME copper, zinc pare losses, others little change.

text.p: Base metals had varying degrees of success on Tuesday in recovering from Monday's fund-led sell off, with copper and zinc making the best progress.
Buoyed by a stock drawdown and trade interest, benchmark three months copper climbed $14 to finish the afternoon kerb at $2,292 per tonne.
But the lower prices were not enough to lure long-awaited Chinese buying, a physical trader said.
Chartwise, copper still looked vulnerable and may have to head still lower before posting further advances, analysts said.

"Copper does not look bad, and the close at these levels suggests an upward bias. But it will have to finish above $2,320 before it starts looking like a reversal," said Martin Squires of brokers Rudolf Wolff.
Waterside Futures said in a report that copper should descend to about $2,217.
This represented a Fibonacci retracement of 61.8 percent from recent highs of $2,442 after the 38.2 percent support at $2,303 gave way, the broker's WaveTrack report said.
Zinc similarly climbed $13 to finish at $1,260, after tumbling $20 on Monday.
Other metals were mixed, with consolidation in relatively narrow ranges the overarching theme across the board.

"The metals have been recovering today from the sell off, with some bargain hunting and profit taking, but no aggressive fund selling," Squires said. Light fund selling early in the day was absorbed by trade buying.
Aluminium dipped initially, with stocks showing a rise of 2,675 tonnes after Monday's inventory decline.
But for most of the day it consolidated in a tight range, with limited trade buying failing to lift prices above a high of $1,588.
It ended virtually unchanged at $1,582.50, down $0.50.
Lead prices hovered just above the $650 level and ended the kerb $3 firmer at $653. A trader noted that lead saw good buying at Monday's lows, in which consumers covered about half of their needs.

"They came in around the lows in the $640s, they didn't want to miss the boat," the trader said, adding that consumers were waiting for further price dips towards $625 to do their next round of buying.
Lead may still be overpriced considering the disappointing winter battery replacement season, but summer business would kick in some time next month and help support prices, the trader said.
Nickel edged barely higher to $7,305, up $15, while tin climbed $20, to $5,740.
Alloy was quiet but was last indicated weaker at $1,470/$1,474, versus $1,485.
